To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the human-livestoek-wildlife interface is an important source of zoonotic tuberculosis, that there is a lack of awareness of this interface in many countries, that there are important gaps in knowledge about transmission of tuberculosis between livestock and wildlife and that a One Health approach is essential to address the issues.
tuberculosis is a disease of global significance, that it is a disease of humans, livestock and wildlife, and that it is a One Health disease.
In summary, our research is concerned with

(1) the role of livestock and wildlife in the transmission of TB; (2) the role of wildlife in maintaining the TB reservoir; (3) the role of human-wildlife contact in transmission of TB to humans; (4) the impact of TB on wildlife and the ecosystem; and (5) the use of trans-disciplinary teams for addressing the problem.
the following questions: (1) How can a One Health approach be used to understand and manage the human-livestic-wildlife interface?
the following questions: What are the threats of TB to humans, livestock and wildlife?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the One Health concept is a necessary and effective approach to addressing disease in the shrinking world.
TB is a complex disease that is not easily controlled.
the One Health approach is the only viable approach to address the complex problems of zoonoses at the interface of human and wildlife.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the One Health approach is not only a concept but a necessity for managing and protecting the public health and animal health of our shrinking world.
the human-livestic-wildlife interface is an increasingly important area for research and management of zoonotic disease.

the more we understand the complex interconnections among humans, wildlife and livestock, and the more we can work together to address the issues, the greater the likelihood that we can protect the health of all species.
The main takeaway from our work is that

a One Health approach to TB control and elimination is essential to ensure a comprehensive understanding of the epidemiology of the disease, the identification of reservoirs and the development of effective interventions.
the use of transdisciplinarity and One Health is critical to understanding the complex nature of zoonotic infections.

the use of transboundary teams can help to identify and manage emerging diseases, and that a transdisciplinary approach can provide a framework to identify and address issues at the human-livetstock-wildlife interface.
